accuracy.reason: All eight objectives are correctly scoped to an authoritative database and cache-aside copies. Hits can be stale; deletion races, TTL age limits, local/shared access scope and outage overload are explicit. No automatic freshness or fallback-safety guarantee.

evidence.quote: Saving the price and removing the copy are separate steps. A reader can fetch $20 before the update, pause, then refill $20 after removal. The next cache hit still returns $20. Removal can also fail.
A hit can still return outdated data. Presence in a cache does not prove that the value matches its source.

mechanisms.reason: Hit/miss actors and costs are traceable. The old-read/pause/write/delete/refill ordering explains stale resurrection, and request coalescing explains reduced source work. Diagrams correctly separate hit/miss paths and source/cache versions.

evidence.quote: Many requests miss the same key together and repeat its database lookup. Coalescing requests lets concurrent readers share one in-progress lookup.

coherence.reason: Reuse benefit leads to read paths, ownership/keys, changing values, entry removal, placement and overload. The final cache-or-not decision uses those mechanisms; every card objective and prerequisite is supported.

evidence.quote: Include the inputs that change the answer. Reusing one person's private result for another person is a data leak.

decisions.reason: Includes both worthwhile repeated work and single-use rejection, required key dimensions, freshness-critical source validation, local/shared failure trade-offs and bounded fallback. Measurement includes latency, source load, hit ratio and miss cost.

evidence.quote: Choose results that are expensive enough to obtain, frequently reused and able to tolerate a defined amount of staleness. Keep freshness-critical decisions tied to authoritative data.

A cache outage can turn most reads into database traffic. Limit fallback work to what the database can handle; reject excess requests or serve older data only where the application permits stale results.

clarity.reason: Cache-aside, hit/miss, key, invalidation, TTL, eviction and stampede are defined plainly. Concrete values clarify the race; local/shared consequences distinguish losing cache access from necessarily losing the application.

evidence.quote: Restarting one API process discards its local cache; other processes keep their copies. If the shared cache is unreachable, every API server using it loses access to those cached entries.

outcomes.reason: All five criteria met from slides 1–3: learner transfers key dimensions to station/language, reuses costly guides on hits, traces application-owned database fetch/fill on misses and accounts for lookup/fill/storage costs. No blanket speedup claim.

All four criteria met from slides 4 and 8: C gets old hours because A refills after deletion; commit/delete cannot cancel A’s saved value or guarantee freshness. Reading the authoritative source avoids this specified stale cache response, without invented coherence machinery.

All four criteria met from slides 2 and 5: 12:03 stale hit, 12:11 expired miss, 12:05 evicted miss; TTL bounds entry lifetime rather than residence/source freshness, and later requests perform loads. Time and space removal are distinguished.

All five criteria met from slide 6: local copies survive another instance’s deletion, shared entry matches the explicitly no-concurrent-fill goal, local versus network access and common outage/cost are explained. Cache-access loss is not asserted to imply application failure or database synchronization.

All five criteria met from slide 7: one pending refill shared by waiters reduces duplication; 10000/s fallback exceeds 500/s capacity; total admitted source work is capped and excess rejected. Optional stale reuse is explicitly conditional on an independently accessible copy and 60-second age; the valid rejection path does not rely on such an unspecified copy.

All five criteria met from slides 1 and 8: rejects useless post-read fills, explains no later reuse plus cheap source/headroom, names costs, and conditions reconsideration on repeated expensive or capacity-constrained work with staleness requirements.

sourceChecks.claim: Opened Microsoft caching guidance: repeated expensive/static reads can benefit; copy costs remain. Database authority is an explicit lesson assumption.
Opened Microsoft cache-aside steps: application lookup, source fetch and fill/return verified; source/cache consistency is not guaranteed.
Opened caching guidance keyspace and private/shared cache sections. Including response-varying inputs follows key identity; omitting private identity can reuse another person’s value.

Opened cache-aside write/invalidate flow and consistency caveat. The precise stale-refill counterexample is a valid operation-order derivation of separate reads/fills, not an extra atomicity guarantee from the source.

Opened Redis eviction policies including noeviction and approximated LRU. Expiration additionally checked at https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/expire/. Removal affects the key, not source refresh or freshness of previously fetched content.

Opened AWS primary article, redirected to https://builder.aws.com/content/3K9TeXp6strMiJ4vhakpRD7BQWO/caching-challenges-and-strategies: independent on-box copies, external common cache and operational/failure costs verified.

Inspected AWS request-coalescing and load-shedding sections: single pending source request and capped fallback reduce overload; cache-disabled testing is recommended. Lesson does not assume an unreachable stale value is readable.
Opened Microsoft guidance and AWS reuse discussion: low reuse can erase benefits, freshness and miss costs matter, and measurements justify adoption. No performance benchmark is asserted.
